title: Coriolis Force in Rotating Frames of Reference
short_intro: The Coriolis force is a fictitious inertial force experienced by objects in motion relative to a non-inertial reference frame rotating at a constant angular velocity. It acts perpendicularly to both the velocity vector of the particle and the axis of rotation of the frame.

exam_scope.tgt_core: Qualitative understanding of non-inertial frames, direction of Coriolis force, effects on falling bodies, and basic conceptual differences between centrifugal and Coriolis forces.
exam_scope.pgt_extension: Complete mathematical derivation from rotating coordinate transformations, quantitative calculation of deflection of freely falling bodies, winds, and Foucault pendulum principles.

prerequisites: Newton's laws of motion in non-inertial reference frames

concept_notes.heading: Origin of the Coriolis Force
bullets: Arises due to the time derivative of rotating unit vectors in a non-inertial reference frame.
Does not perform work on the particle because the force vector is always perpendicular to the velocity vector in the rotating frame.
Depends linearly on the mass, velocity of the particle in the rotating frame, and the angular velocity of the frame.

concept_notes.heading: Direction and Magnitude
bullets: Given mathematically by the vector expression F = -2m(omega x v), where v is the relative velocity.
In the Northern Hemisphere, the Coriolis force deflects moving objects to the right of their direction of motion.
In the Southern Hemisphere, the deflection is to the left of the direction of motion.

concept_notes.heading: Terrestrial Effects
bullets: Responsible for the counter-clockwise rotation of cyclones in the Northern Hemisphere and clockwise in the Southern Hemisphere.
Causes a freely falling body dropped from a height to be deflected eastward due to the Earth's rotation.
Zero at the equator where the rotation axis is parallel to the local vertical, and maximum at the poles.

concept_notes.heading: Distinction from Centrifugal Force
bullets: Centrifugal force depends on the position vector from the axis of rotation, whereas Coriolis force depends on the velocity vector.
Centrifugal force is radially outward, while Coriolis force is transverse to the motion.
Both are apparent forces introduced to apply Newton's laws in rotating coordinate systems.

derivations.title: Transformation of Velocity and Acceleration to a Rotating Frame
derivations.conditions: Frame rotating with constant angular velocity omega
steps: Express a position vector r in terms of rotating unit vectors (i', j', k'): r = x'i' + y'j' + z'k'.
Take the time derivative in the inertial frame using operator identity: (dr/dt)_inertial = (dr/dt)_rotating + omega x r.
Apply the operator to the velocity vector v_rotating to obtain the acceleration in the inertial frame: a_inertial = a_rotating + 2(omega x v_rotating) + omega x (omega x r).
derivations.result: a_rotating = a_inertial - 2(omega x v) - omega x (omega x r)

derivations.title: Deflection of a Freely Falling Body
derivations.conditions: Body dropped from height h at latitude lambda in Northern Hemisphere
steps: Write the equation of motion in the rotating earth frame: a = g_eff - 2(omega x v).
For zeroth-order motion, falling vertically under gravity: v_z = -gt, so z = h - (1/2)gt^2.
Substitute v into the Coriolis term: F_coriolis / m = -2(omega x v). Evaluating components shows an eastward acceleration equal to 2 omega v_z cos(lambda).
Integrate the eastward acceleration twice with respect to time to find the total eastward displacement.
derivations.result: Eastward deflection delta = (1/3) omega g t^3 cos(lambda) = (1/3) omega cos(lambda) sqrt(8h^3 / g)

graphs_and_experiments.title: Deflection of Projectile on Rotating Disk
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A top-down view of a rotating disk with a straight line drawn by an inertial observer versus the curved trajectory traced by an observer on the disk.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Illustrates how a straight path in an inertial frame appears deflected to the right or left due to the Coriolis effect in the rotating frame.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Frequently used in conceptual multiple-choice questions regarding apparent trajectory curving.

graphs_and_experiments.title: Foucault Pendulum Plane Rotation
graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A circular arena showing successive precession angles of the swinging plane of a heavy pendulum over hours.
graphs_and_experiments.interpretation: Demonstrates the non-inertial nature of the Earth's frame as the apparent rotation of the pendulum plane confirms Earth's axial rotation.
graphs_and_experiments.exam_use: Asked in descriptive or advanced TGT/PGT questions concerning experimental proof of Earth's rotation.

graphs_and_experiments.what_to_draw: A plot of Coriolis acceleration magnitude against latitude lambda from 0 to 90 degrees for a fixed particle velocity.

solved_numericals.question: A body of mass 2 kg is moving with a velocity of 10 m/s from west to east at the equator. If the angular velocity of the Earth is 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s, calculate the magnitude of the Coriolis force.
solution_steps: Identify given values: m = 2 kg, v = 10 m/s, omega = 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s.
At the equator, the velocity vector is perpendicular to the Earth's rotation axis, so theta = 90 degrees.
Use formula F_cor = 2 m v omega sin(90) = 2 * 2 * 10 * (7.27 x 10^-5) * 1.

solved_numericals.question: An object is dropped from a height of 100 meters at a place with latitude 30 degrees north. Given g = 9.8 m/s^2 and omega = 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s, find its eastward deflection.
solution_steps: Recall formula for eastward deflection: delta = (1/3) * omega * cos(lambda) * sqrt(8 h^3 / g).
Substitute values: h = 100 m, lambda = 30 degrees (cos(30) = sqrt(3)/2), g = 9.8 m/s^2, omega = 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s.
Calculate time of fall t = sqrt(2h / g) = sqrt(200 / 9.8) = 4.517 s.

solved_numericals.question: Find the magnitude of the Coriolis acceleration for a vehicle moving due North at 72 km/h at a latitude of 45 degrees.
solution_steps: Convert velocity to SI units: v = 72 km/h = 72 * (5/18) = 20 m/s.
Identify Earth angular velocity omega = 7.27 x 10^-5 rad/s and latitude lambda = 45 degrees.
The effective vertical component of angular velocity contributing to horizontal Coriolis force is omega_z = omega * sin(lambda).
Coriolis acceleration a_cor = 2 * omega_z * v = 2 * omega * sin(45) * v.

assumptions_and_limitations: The rotating frame has a constant angular velocity vector omega (d(omega)/dt = 0).
Applicable only within non-relativistic mechanics where v is much less than the speed of light.
Assumes the Earth can be treated as a uniformly rotating reference frame, ignoring local crustal anomalies or non-spherical perturbations for basic derivations.

common_misconceptions.wrong: The Coriolis force does physical work on moving objects because it accelerates them.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Coriolis force does zero work on a particle.
common_misconceptions.why: Since the Coriolis force is always perpendicular to the instantaneous velocity vector in the rotating frame, the instantaneous power (F . v) is identically zero.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Water drains clockwise or counter-clockwise in washbasins strictly due to the Coriolis force.
common_misconceptions.correct: The Coriolis force is too weak to affect small-scale phenomena like draining sinks.
common_misconceptions.why: Initial asymmetries, container geometry, and residual angular momentum dominate washbasin vortex directions; Coriolis force only dictates large-scale meteorological systems like typhoons.

common_misconceptions.wrong: Coriolis force is a real fundamental force of nature.
common_misconceptions.correct: Coriolis force is a fictitious or inertial force.
common_misconceptions.why: It arises purely as a mathematical consequence of formulating Newtonian mechanics in an accelerated (rotating) coordinate system.

quick_revision: Coriolis force formula is F_cor = -2m(omega x v).
It causes rightward deflection in the Northern Hemisphere and leftward in the Southern Hemisphere.
It does no work as it remains perpendicular to the relative velocity vector.
Maximum at the poles and zero at the equator.
Responsible for the rotation direction of large-scale weather cyclones and Foucault pendulum precession.
